Subject: platypus.

reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module to build a platypus model in Studio Ghibli style using the SDK, thinking through realistic proportions and a soft, warm, hand-painted aesthetic with gentle glossy eyes.

I'm mapping out which builder functions to use for limbs, curves, paint, and shading, then sketching a skeleton layout: body along the z-axis with short splayed legs, webbed feet, a flat duck bill, and a paddle-shaped tail, posed resting on the ground.

Now I'm defining the joint hierarchy, starting with hips as the root and building a spine chain with catmull curve points running from rump to head.

Simplifying the neck to a single named joint parented to the last spine joint, aimed forward, with a separate head joint — assigning roles "neck" and "head" accordingly. For the tail, I'm building a backward-curving chain from the hips with decreasing height values.

Now I'm planning the body mesh as a sweep along a path from the rump through the chest, bound to a bone chain spanning tail, hips, and spine so the mesh deforms with the skeleton.

Working out the radius profile...

For color, I'll go with a Ghibli-style warm brown back and lighter cream-tan belly with countershading, plus adding fur tufts along the back and flanks for texture.

Now I'm thinking through how to tint those fur tuft cards: I'll use a grayscale gradient tuft tinted by the coat's countershade color, so the texture reads correctly without needing separate colored assets.

For the bill, I want a flat, wide, rounded slate-grey shape with a lighter tip and nostrils near the front, Ghibli-style. I'm building it as a loft from stations running forward along the skull, tapering width and height toward the tip, though I'm unsure whether the loft cross-section defaults to a rounded box or ellipse.

As a safer alternative, I'm considering extruding a bird's-eye outline of the bill shape in the x-z plane instead, working out the thickness axis from the cross product of the chosen outline directions.

That stepped layering fits the blocky puppet look I'm going for, so I'll use the main extrude with a bevel just under half the thickness for rounded edges, then work out the bill outline coordinates to get the right spatulate widening shape and length.

I'm scaling things stylistically larger than real proportions, so I'm placing the head around z≈0.25 with a sphere radius near 0.065, and the bill extending from z=0.29 to about 0.40, keeping half-width around 0.04 so the body stays roughly 0.18 wide overall. I just need to check that the smoothing level won't cause corner-cutting conflicts given how closely spaced the outline points are.

To stay safe, I'll switch to smoothing 1 with denser outlines (~12 points) rather than smoothing 2. Now I'm working out the lower bill and jaw joint placement relative to the head center, trying to pin down local coordinates for the head joint and its forward-aim direction in rest pose.

Switching to model-space geometry: jaw joint parented to the head, with the upper bill plate thicker and higher than the narrower, thinner lower bill plate, while the skull sphere sits behind and overlaps the bill base to avoid any gap.

For eyes, I'm thinking platypus eyes are small and set in a groove to the sides of the head behind the bill, but for the Ghibli style I want big shiny round eyes with highlights — likely using a decal with an eye texture (dark pupil, iris ring, highlights) projected onto a flattened disc facing outward from the skull.

I also want to add pale cream eye patches around the eyes using a small decal ellipse, since platypuses have light patches near the eyes, plus a suggestion of eyelids drawn directly into the texture rather than modeled geometrically. I'm now working out the eye placement relative to the head center and skull scale.

For positioning, I'm setting the eye azimuth around ±55° and elevation near 22-25°, computing the hit point and normal on the skull surface to orient the decal, and mirroring across sides so s=1 maps to the +X side correctly. As for ears, platypuses don't have external ears, so I'll skip modeling them and instead consider adding subtle dark groove marks behind the eyes to suggest ear slits.

Now I'm placing small flattened spherical nostrils near the bill tip using explicit coordinates just above the bill's top surface, slightly embedded for a natural look. I'm also planning bill details like a central ridge line and a raised shield fold at the base of the bill, possibly as a thin rim or flattened ring in a slightly darker tone.

Adding fur-fringed skin fold detail around the bill base...

Setting up the leg geometry now — short laterally projecting limbs with webbed feet, using IK chains to position hip, knee, and foot joints for a realistic platypus stance with elbows splayed outward and feet flat on the ground.

For the feet, I'm planning a webbed fan shape plus five small toe capsules with claws, deciding whether to budget separate joints per toe across all four feet given the overall joint count limit.

I'm working out the toe and web heights so everything meets the floor cleanly: toes get radius 0.006 centered at y=0.006 so their bottom touches zero, and I'm aligning the webbing's thickness and vertical position to match that same floor contact.

For the hind feet, I'm noting that platypus rear feet angle backward-outward when swimming but point out/forward at rest, and they carry less webbing than the front feet.

I'll give the hind feet a smaller web, pointing them outward at roughly 75° from center and adding a tiny ankle spur to reference the male platypus's venomous spur, while front toes fan out from around 35°. Now I'm working out the toe fan placement formula to space individual digits around that central direction angle.

Each toe gets its own joint pair (base and tip) parented to the limb's wrist joint, positioned along its fan direction, so I need to confirm which named joint in the limb chain represents the wrist for proper parenting.

For attaching legs to the spine, I'm mapping shoulder and hip positions to the nearest spine segment based on z-coordinate: shoulders at z=0.13 fall within spine3's span, while hips at z=-0.1 align closer to the hips joint itself.

For the leg skinning, I'm sweeping tube geometry along each arm chain with tapering radius, and checking that shoulder attachment points sit just inside the body surface radius so the legs appear to emerge naturally from the torso.

Lengths need lengthening to 0.07 and 0.065 for a visible elbow bend, with the joint pointing outward and slightly upward. For the hind leg I'm mirroring the same setup with the root and target positions flipped in z, using similar bend hints, and thinking through how chains built from polyline point arrays handle intermediate knots.

For the tail, I want it flat and broad like a platypus or beaver -- paddle-shaped with a wide, rounded cross-section. I'm designing a sweep along a separate tail chain (distinct from the body sweep) using an elliptical radius profile that stays wide but thin, tapering slightly toward the tip, starting from the hips and running backward in z.

I'll split this into two separate sweeps: a body sweep running from the tail root forward through the hips and spine, and a separate tail paddle sweep that tapers with its own flattened elliptical cross-section, starting hidden inside the body.

Working out the tail paddle shape...

I'm also fixing the tail's vertical position so it droops down toward the ground rather than floating, lowering the y-coordinates along its path to make it drag naturally like a platypus tail.

Checking the body path's rear point against the tail bone shows a small y mismatch, but since the mesh just rides along the bone's projection, this slight offset won't cause visible distortion. I'm also noting I should add coarse fur texture cards to the tail to match the platypus's rough tail covering, and confirming the spine chain can keep default rotation settings.

I'm defining the neck and head joints as children of the spine chain's last segment, positioning them so the body's front cap aligns with where the skull sphere will sit, then assigning chain roles like "spine," "tail," "arm," and "leg" to keep the rig semantically organized.

Now I'm sizing the skull as a flattened sphere scaled down in height to match a platypus's low, streamlined head shape, adjusting its vertical position so its underside meets the body's front cap without floating above the ground.

I'm also framing a fur ruff ring around the base of the bill, and setting up the fur coat paint with a Ghibli-style palette blending warm browns on the back and tan tones on the belly using noise-based mixing.

Writing shader paint logic...

Now I'm adding pale cream cheek patches near the eyes as decals, and making sure the layering offset avoids z-fighting with other decals at the same spot.

For the eye itself, I'm sketching an SVG design with a dark iris, brown ring, and layered highlights to give it that Ghibli-style glossy stylized look, sized a bit larger than a real platypus eye would be. Then I'm designing fur tuft cards as grey-gradient SVG blades that get tinted by the fur color paint system.

Now I'm working out the scatter distribution for fur cards across body regions — figuring out counts and minimum spacing per area so the density looks plausible without overcrowding the surface.

Settling on card sizing, lean angle, and bend parameters so the cards flop flat like shingles toward the back, producing a believable fur silhouette, then estimating triangle counts to keep the mesh budget reasonable.

For color, I'll make the tuft tint a lightened version of the base coat color by mixing it toward a warm cream tone, so tufts read as subtly lighter fur rather than flat matching skin, and I'm also considering excluding card placement near the belly where normals point downward.

I don't think the scene needs extra elements like grass or whiskers to sell the Ghibli charm—better to keep focus on the platypus itself, but I want to add a texture detail to the bill: tiny dark speckles mimicking the sensor pores using a cell-noise pattern, plus a softer pink tint along the bill's rim for warmth.

Now I'm adding a subtle bill ridge and nostril detail, and considering a thin lighter flange around the bill base for extra dimensionality.

I'm skipping the shield detail and instead working out the precise jaw geometry—sizing the upper and lower bill extrusions and positioning them so there's a small realistic gap between them, while checking that the upper bill properly meets the skull front position.

Realizing the skull placement needs adjustment: if the head center sits too far forward, the bill barely emerges past the skull surface, leaving too short a visible bill. I'm shifting the skull center back so the bill has roughly 0.12 total length with enough of it visible beyond the head.

I'm now placing the jaw joint and lower bill extrusion, deciding the chin mass can just be part of the skull sphere rather than a separate piece, and positioning the lower bill extrude with its orientation vectors and thickness so opening the jaw rotates it cleanly around the pivot without weird intersection with the skull.

Writing bill outline coordinates...

I'll scale the bill points down proportionally for the lower bill, check the width ratios between bill and body stay reasonable, and set up a bevel with small thickness and a few steps. Then I'm adding a second, smaller dome extrusion on top of the upper bill, offsetting its thickness slightly above the main bill surface for a layered look.

For the dome, I'll use a tighter outline scale and position it so it sits raised above the main bill, mimicking the ridge on a platypus bill. Then I'm placing small nostril details at the top of the dome using scaled spheres positioned to stay embedded within the bill geometry, colored dark to contrast with the bill paint.

Now I'm setting up the skull as its own part using a scaled sphere geometry positioned at the head anchor, applying the coat paint across its surface. I'm figuring out eye placement by calculating azimuth and elevation angles relative to the skull's scaled radius.

I need these ring items to attach to the head bone rather than floating loose, so I'll bind the cards to `bone: head` for rigidity. I'm also thinking I should use only a partial arc of the ring, maybe from 60 to 300 degrees, to avoid the bill area and cover just the sides and bottom of the cheek.

For orientation, I realize full ring angle 0 should align with world up, with angles going counterclockwise around the Z axis — so a complete ring works fine here, like fluffy fur framing the base of the platypus's bill. Since ring items face outward along their radial axis, I can lean them toward the flow direction to sweep them backward, using a moderate lean angle and small card sizes so the top and bottom pieces at the wider radius sit correctly.

For head coverage, I'm scattering roughly 70 small cards across the skull surface for fur texture, filtering out any that point too far downward or that fall too close to the eyes or bill region so they don't poke out awkwardly over the face. I'm checking hit positions against the eye locations and excluding the front bill area using simple position-based conditions.

I also want to add small spike details near the ankles of the hind legs using a cone-spike helper anchored to the ankle bone for a subtle spur effect.

Then I'm planning tiny claw spikes at each toe tip, roughly a dozen of them, with a dark brownish color, and thinking through toe and webbing colors—leathery greyish-brown toes with lighter pinkish-tan webbing, possibly adding a radial streak or gradient pattern across the webs to mimic vein texture.

I'm checking whether too many separately painted parts will overload the texture sheet, but since each part gets its own chart it should be fine; estimating that with roughly half a square meter of total painted surface at a 1024px texture, the density works out to about 0.8mm per texel, which seems reasonable.

Bumping the paint sheet to 2048 would give sharper detail for small pore features, and since the atlas allows up to 4096 this stays comfortably within limits, so I'll go with 2048. For the webbed foot shape, I'm planning to build it as a polygon in model space using a slab helper that turns a flat outline into a thin closed prism, starting the point list from the wrist.

Laying out the fan points...

Checking the endpoints span 168° with the closing chord between P_end and P0 passing close to W but not through it, keeping the polygon simple and star-shaped around W.

Now I'm adjusting the slab and toe placement to avoid overlap -- shifting the slab center to y=0.0055 with thickness spanning 0.003 to 0.008, and setting toe tubes at y=0.006 with radius 0.006 so they sit flatter against the web, while targeting the limb's foot position around y=0.007.

But checking the wrist leg tube, I realize if it sweeps down to y=0.007 with a radius of 0.015, it'll actually sink below the floor to y=-0.008, which exceeds the acceptable tolerance of about 0.0034 relative to height — that's a real problem I need to fix for the limb's lowest point.

So I'm reworking this: taper the leg tube to a smaller end radius (~0.007-0.008) and raise the wrist joint to y≈0.008, accounting for how the round cap extends beyond the path end along the tangent direction, which should bring the actual lowest point closer to zero without piercing the floor.

I'm also noting that platypus legs should look stouter, not spindly, so I'll want to adjust the taper curve, while confirming the tail tip geometry (with its own radius and round cap) stays just above ground level too.

For the tail paddle shape, I'm sketching width values across seven key points along its length, making it widest around two-thirds to three-quarters of the way out before narrowing to the rounded tip, roughly matching a real platypus tail's proportions.

I'm also checking that the tail's cross-section radius blends smoothly into the body's rear taper, and thinking through using a coarser, darker fur texture for the tail to reflect its distinctive coat.

For the body's coloring, I'm adding a cream-silver belly patch reminiscent of a real platypus while keeping the overall shape blocky, consistent with a puppet built from simple primitives. I'm deciding against extra whimsical additions like leaves, though I'm considering a few subtle water droplets catching light on the fur.

I'll skip some flourishes but keep the "wow" factor through painted rim lights, sparkly eyes, fur tufts, and veined webbed feet with visible pores. I'm also adding a pale cream fur fringe along the belly sides using the same card technique, just tinted cream, placed along the lower flanks. I'm deciding against eyebrow ridges for now, and moving into defining the parameters for the card-placement function that will handle sizing, bending, variation, and color.

Still writing SVG tuft shapes...

Adding brown shading at the bottom of the eye with an ellipse, then checking that it stays within the circle's bounds so nothing overflows into the transparent area.

I'm adding highlight circles and a curved lid stroke along the top, double-checking the lid arc stays inside the main circle, then sketching a separate eye patch shape using layered cream-colored ellipses for a soft but defined edge.

Now I'm sizing and tilting the eye and patch decals, making sure the decal direction uses the hit's surface normal with a fallback for null hits, and considering small dark slit decals behind the eyes for ear grooves.

For leg fur, I'm blending the coat color into a darker tone lower down using a gradient keyed on vertical position, and sweeping the arms with the same leg paint color for consistency.

Skipping elbow/knee ruffs for now, and planning a foot builder function that handles toe joints parented to the wrist, using inferred chain types from the SDK rather than explicit imports to avoid typing issues.

Writing toe fan loop...

Switching to capsules for rounder toe tips instead of flat-ended rods, tapering the radius from base to tip, then adding small clawed spikes extending just past each toe end.

Choosing darker claw and toe colors for a softer Ghibli-style look, then tallying up parts: 4 feet × 5 toes gives 20 joints, capsules, and claws plus 4 slabs, though I need to pad the part count toward my 100+ target while keeping the total code length manageable. I'm also considering adding radial vein patterns on the foot pads by computing angles around the center point to create darker toe-aligned streaks.

Settling on using a sine-based threshold to create radiating vein lines from the wrist across the webbing, then setting specific angle, spread, and length parameters for hind versus front feet, with the front feet having broader, more fanned-out webbing between toes.

Checking the body width tapering near the head and shoulders, I'm tuning rx/ry parameters so the platypus stays stocky but narrows appropriately toward the head and cap regions.

Now I'm defining the spine's vertebrae path to match the body curve, aligning hip and spine joint positions with the body's y-path points so the skeleton follows the same silhouette, then starting the tail root position off the hips.

Checking total length though—tail plus body plus bill adds up to around 0.85, which is too elongated compared to a real platypus's 0.5-0.6 overall length. I'm considering whether to apply a uniform scale factor to compress everything proportionally, or just accept the stylized elongated proportions as a design choice.

Let me compress the body further: shrinking to a chubbier, shorter form with body from -0.16 to 0.14, tail to -0.30, head center at 0.165, and bill tip to 0.31, giving a total length around 0.61. That feels more proportionate and cute, so I'll redo all the coordinates with these tighter dimensions.

Working out the exact spine and body path coordinates...

I'm checking the tail radii values at each sample point against the floor to make sure the tail never clips below ground, verifying the x/y radius pairs stay consistent along the taper toward the tip.

I'll try tapering RX more gradually near the end, like 0.064, 0.058, 0.04, so the plan view reads as rounded rather than abruptly flat, then decide between a flat or round cap depending on whether the dome radius risks dipping below the floor.

Since the elliptical cross-section is uncertain, I'll just raise the tail tip slightly to y=0.02 so the dome's lowest point stays at or above the floor, giving the tail path a natural curve: 0.082, 0.068, 0.048, 0.03, 0.02. Now I'm moving on to the head, setting the skull center and scale dimensions.

Working through the skull-to-bill transition, I realize the total body length comes out to about 0.64m with my current bill length, which feels too long for this stylized platypus, so I'm scaling the bill outline down to a length of 0.112 instead. Adjusting the bill outline coordinates...

I'm positioning the upper and lower bill segments at slightly offset y-centers so there's just a sliver of a gap between them, and checking that the skull ellipse's span overlaps correctly with where the bill sits on the lower-front of the head, matching real platypus anatomy.

Adjusting the lower bill scale at that pivot point (0.92, tip around 0.303), then checking the dome extrusion dimensions for the upper bill to get a slight 4mm rise above the base profile.

Working out the nostril placement, eye angles relative to the head center, and the leg geometry—checking shoulder-to-foot distances against the segment lengths to make sure the bend angles stay reasonable, then verifying the body radius at that z-position.

Toe tip clears body edge fine, and front/hind feet don't collide with their torso contact points. Adding a small pale spur near the hind wrist joint, positioned slightly behind and under the bone. Considering small brow bumps on the head as an extra detail, while skipping fur tufts at the elbows for now.

For the eyes, I'm weighing options between a flat decal, a bulging bead sphere, or a textured sphere wrapping the eye drawing -- leaning toward a simple dark bead sphere embedded at the surface combined with a flat decal for the eye art, since a fully wrapped textured sphere adds too much complexity.

I'll keep the eye as a decal only, adding thin dark brow arcs above each eye in the SVG, and I'm satisfied the chest fur ruff is already covered by the belly tufts. For a bit of extra polish, I'm thinking about adding a subtle glossy highlight stripe on the bill using a smoothstep blend near the top with a light bluish-gray sheen color, then moving on to building the body surfaces -- sweeping the body tube, wrapping it into a surface, and setting up scatter hits for the card placement.
